opus-5.5.text:
I think the chatbot is a fairly limited form factor relative to what these models can actually do. When you chat with a model, the interaction is bottlenecked by you: you ask a question, it answers, you read, you think, you ask again. The model's capability is gated by how fast and how well a human can prompt it and consume its output. That's a very narrow channel.

What's exciting about these models is that they can increasingly act. They can use tools, write and run code, browse, and work on something for minutes or hours without a human in the loop at every step. When you squeeze that into a chat window, you're treating something that could be a coworker like a very smart search box.

There's also the question of what generates value. A lot of chat usage is people asking things they're curious about, which is nice, but most economic value in the world comes from doing tasks: software engineering, research, operations, a long tail of work across organizations. Those tasks are long-horizon, need context, and need the model to interact with an environment. A single conversational turn doesn't capture that.

So for me the interesting direction is moving from "AI answers your question" to "AI completes your task." That changes how we evaluate models too. Instead of asking whether a response is good, you ask whether the job got done, which is a much more grounded signal. The chatbot was a great first product and an amazing way to show the world what language models can do, but I don't think it's the end state. It's more like the command line before the GUI: one interface among many, not the final one.

r001.rationale: The response calls chat a “fairly limited form factor” relative to what models can do, and explains that models can act, use tools, and complete longer tasks beyond the narrow question-and-answer loop.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the chatbot is unsatisfying because it puts the burden of the work back on the human. You open a text box, you type a question, you get an answer, and then you have to decide what to do with it. The model only acts when you prompt it, and it only sees what you paste into the window. So most of the actual work, gathering context, running things, checking results, iterating, that still falls on you. The model becomes a very smart consultant you have to keep walking back and forth to.

That's a strange way to use something this capable. What I care about is agents, models that take actions in an environment, observe what happens, and keep going. The interesting thing about a language model is not that it can produce text, it's that text can be a general interface to tools, to code, to the web, to other people. When you put it in a chat box you collapse all of that into a single modality, one turn at a time, where the environment is just a human reading and typing.

There's also a feedback problem. In a chatbot, the signal the model gets is whether the human liked the response. That's a weak signal, it rewards sounding good more than being right. When the model is actually doing a task, say fixing a bug and running the tests, there's ground truth. It either works or it doesn't. That's the kind of environment where you can really learn and really measure progress, and it's why I spent so much time on things like SWE-bench and tau-bench rather than on better conversation.

And honestly, from a product point of view, chat is where we started because it was the easiest thing to build around a model that wasn't reliable enough to act on its own. It was a reasonable first interface, but it was a constraint, not a destination. As models get better at long-horizon tasks, I think the natural shape is less like talking to something and more like delegating to it. You describe the outcome you want, and it goes and does the work, comes back when it needs you. The chatbot will probably survive as one surface, but it shouldn't be the way we think about what these systems are for.

r001.rationale: The response says chat is a constraint for a system capable of acting through tools, code, and other environments, reducing those abilities to one-turn text exchanges.

astra-6.text:
I think the chatbot is useful, but it puts a lot of the burden on the user. You have to know what to ask, provide the relevant context, judge the answer, and then take that answer somewhere else to actually do something. The model produces text, but you’re still responsible for moving the task forward.

If I want to solve a programming problem, for example, having a conversation about the code is only part of the work. I also need to inspect files, make changes, run tests, and understand what failed. A more useful system would participate in that whole process, using feedback from the environment to decide what to do next.

So what I find unsatisfying is the gap between getting an answer and getting something done. Conversation can be a good way to communicate intent or clarify a decision. But I don’t think every step of working with an AI should require another message from the user.

r001.rationale: The response says chatbots reduce the model to producing text while leaving users to carry tasks forward, and argues AI should participate in the whole work process. This clearly conveys a mismatch between chatbot use and the broader capabilities of AI models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think chat is a useful interface, but it puts a lot of the burden on the human. You have to formulate the task, provide the context, read the answer, and then figure out what to do next. If the task takes ten steps, you may have to keep prompting the model through all ten steps. The model can generate a good response, but you’re still managing the whole process.

What I find more interesting is whether an AI can take a goal, interact with an environment, and make progress on its own. It might need to use a tool, observe the result, realize that something didn’t work, and try again. In that setting, generating text is one part of doing the task.

So the limitation isn’t really the chat box itself. It’s that we often treat producing an answer as the endpoint. For many things I want help with, the endpoint is getting something done.

r001.rationale: The response describes chat’s burden and AI’s ability to act through tools, but it does not clearly say that chatbot use is incongruous with the breadth of AI models’ capabilities. It explicitly says the limitation is not really the chat box itself.
